Immediate effusion.text: Rapid, large-volume swelling within 1-2 hours of injury indicates hemarthrosis from a vascularized intra-articular structure — ACL rupture is the most common cause of acute traumatic knee hemarthrosis, distinguishing it from the delayed, lower-grade effusion typical of an avascular meniscal tear.

Quadriceps inhibition.text: Reflects arthrogenic muscle inhibition (AMI): effusion-driven mechanoreceptor/nociceptor discharge reflexively suppresses the quadriceps motor-neuron pool at the spinal and supraspinal level, a protective mechanism rather than a true contractile weakness — the physiological basis of the weak-but-painless resisted knee extension pattern seen acutely post-ACL.
Quadriceps inhibition.source: Palmieri-Smith et al., quadriceps arthrogenic muscle inhibition literature (PMC4271337)

Giving-way.text: The subjective sensation of the knee buckling during pivoting or deceleration reflects loss of the ACL's role as primary restraint to anterior tibial translation and rotational (pivot) stability, allowing the tibia to sublux under dynamic load.

Genu recurvatum / dynamic valgus.text: Hyperextension laxity (recurvatum) reflects generalized or ACL-specific capsuloligamentous laxity allowing tibial hyperextension, while dynamic valgus collapse (femoral adduction/internal rotation with tibial external rotation on landing) is the biomechanical pattern Hewett identified as the most common mechanism of non-contact ACL injury in female athletes.
Genu recurvatum / dynamic valgus.source: Hewett et al., neuromuscular control and valgus loading predict ACL injury risk (PubMed 15722287)

findings: Resisted knee extension weak & painless (arthrogenic muscle inhibition from effusion, not a true contractile lesion)
Passive tibiofemoral AP glide (Lachman) positive — the definitive test
sttt.interpretation: Resisted knee extension is often weak/painless acutely, reflecting arthrogenic muscle inhibition from effusion rather than a true contractile lesion; the passive tibiofemoral AP glide (Lachman) is the definitive test.

cpa.pattern: "Inhibited, post knee injury/surgery" is the classic post-ACL finding; activate VMO before general quad strengthening. Fascial component (from source): Not applicable acutely; address quads inhibition.

kineticChain.name: Knee Valgus Stress Test

fields.label: Dynamic valgus on squat / single-leg squat / landing

kineticChain.chainEffect: Dynamic valgus on squat/single-leg squat/landing is explicitly documented as "the most common pattern in female ACL injuries"; driven by ankle DF + glute med, not the knee itself.

functionalScreen.name: Single Leg Hop Series
functionalScreen.note: The named return-to-sport functional screen for this exact injury (dynamic valgus + landing mechanics + ACL risk). FMA source note: Lachman/pivot reproduced in function; single-leg hop confidence.

Posterior sag.text: With the knee flexed to 90°, gravity causes the tibia to drop posteriorly relative to the femur when the PCL — the primary static restraint to posterior tibial translation — is deficient; this is the visual basis of the Godfrey/posterior sag sign.

± posterior bruising.text: Ecchymosis over the posterior knee or proximal calf points to the classic PCL mechanism of a direct posteriorly-directed force on the proximal tibia (e.g. dashboard injury), helping confirm mechanism-consistency for PCL injury over other ligamentous patterns.

Posterior tibial droop stance.text: A resting posterior sag of the tibia under gravity or body weight reflects chronic PCL insufficiency, most evident with the knee flexed near 90° where the deficient posterior restraint allows the tibia to translate posteriorly relative to the femur.

findings: Resisted knee flexion may be relatively preserved
Passive posterior tibiofemoral glide (posterior drawer) positive — the definitive test, not a resisted-muscle one
sttt.interpretation: Resisted knee flexion strength may be relatively preserved; the passive posterior tibiofemoral glide (posterior drawer) is the definitive test for PCL injury, not a resisted-muscle one.

cpa.pattern: Popliteus can become "Overactive, posterior-lateral knee pain" secondary to PCL-deficient posterior laxity — screen once the acute phase allows. Fascial component (from source): Posterior capsule.

kineticChain.name: Tibial Rotation Assessment (Screw-Home Mechanism)
kineticChain.chainEffect: PCL laxity can disturb terminal-extension screw-home; check for an "absent screw-home" pattern.

functionalScreen.name: Double Leg Squat (general baseline)
functionalScreen.note: No PCL-specific named functional test exists in this app's library; rely on the joint-play STTT test above as primary. FMA source note: Posterior-drawer load reproduced in function; downhill/decline discomfort.

Joint-line swelling.text: Meniscal tears typically produce a delayed, lower-grade effusion (12-24h post-injury) rather than the immediate hemarthrosis of ACL rupture, reflecting synovial irritation rather than intra-articular bleeding since the inner two-thirds of the meniscus is avascular.

Catching/locking.text: Mechanical catching, or true locking with a block to full extension, occurs when a displaced fragment (classically a bucket-handle tear) becomes physically interposed between the femoral and tibial condyles, obstructing normal joint arthrokinematics.

Quad wasting.text: Reflex quadriceps inhibition secondary to chronic joint irritation and recurrent effusion produces disuse atrophy over the more subacute-to-chronic timeframe typical of a meniscal lesion, most visible in the VMO.

Antalgic.text: A pain-avoidant gait or resting posture reflects protective unloading of the symptomatic tibiofemoral compartment to minimize compressive and rotational joint-line pain generated by the torn meniscal segment.

Avoids full flexion.text: Deep knee flexion markedly increases compressive and shear loading on the posterior horn of the meniscus — the most common tear site — so avoidance of end-range flexion is a protective pattern that helps localize pathology to the meniscus rather than a collateral ligament.

findings: Passive tibial rotation at 90° (McMurray-type) reproduces joint-line pain/click
sttt.interpretation: Strong resisted testing rules out a contractile source; the passive McMurray-type tibial rotation at 90° reproducing joint-line pain/click localizes the lesion to the meniscus.

muscles.name: Hamstrings (medial vs lateral per which meniscus)

cpa.pattern: Hamstrings may guard protectively depending on which meniscus is involved; not a primary compensation-pattern condition. Fascial component (from source): Joint-line capsular fascia.

kineticChain.name: Tibial Rotation Assessment
kineticChain.chainEffect: Passive IR/ER at 90° reproducing joint-line pain is the direct kinetic-chain correlate of a meniscal lesion.

functionalScreen.name: Double Leg Squat
functionalScreen.note: Deep flexion loading reproducing joint-line pain is the functional equivalent of McMurray-type provocation. FMA source note: McMurray/Thessaly & deep squat reproduce joint-line pain.

Medial joint-line tenderness.text: Point tenderness along the medial joint line or the ligament's femoral/tibial attachment localizes the site of fiber disruption, consistent with Cyriax's principle that palpation should reproduce pain directly over the injured structure.
Medial joint-line tenderness.source: Cyriax, Textbook of Orthopaedic Medicine; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.12

Valgus laxity.text: Excess medial joint-line gapping under a valgus load indicates mechanical insufficiency of the MCL, the primary static restraint to valgus stress, especially when laxity is present at 30° flexion where the posterior capsule and ACL contribute minimally.

Valgus-loading alignment.text: A resting or dynamic valgus alignment either reflects the causative forced valgus/external-rotation mechanism or an ongoing inability of the compromised medial structures to resist the physiological valgus moment generated during stance.

findings: Resisted tests around the knee usually painless (ligament, not contractile)
Passive valgus stress (medial gap) at 0°/30° positive — the definitive test
sttt.interpretation: Painless resisted testing rules out a contractile source; passive valgus stress (medial gap) at 0°/30° is the definitive test for MCL sprain.

cpa.pattern: Adductors ("Overactive, medial chain") and the pes anserine group often guard the medial pain secondarily. Fascial component (from source): Medial capsule / pes anserine fascia.

kineticChain.name: Knee Valgus Stress Test

fields.label: Manual valgus stress at 0°/30° (grading MCL laxity)

kineticChain.chainEffect: The direct match, including its manual valgus-stress component at 0°/30° used to grade MCL laxity.

functionalScreen.name: Forward Lunge
functionalScreen.note: Sagittal loading with a valgus-stress component if cutting/lateral movement provokes the medial pain. FMA source note: Valgus stress (0°/30°) & cutting reproduce medial pain.

Lateral joint-line tenderness.text: Point tenderness over the fibular collateral ligament's femoral or fibular-head attachment localizes the lesion, consistent with Cyriax's principle of palpatory localization of a ligamentous injury.
Lateral joint-line tenderness.source: Cyriax, Textbook of Orthopaedic Medicine; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.12

Varus laxity.text: Excess lateral joint-line gapping under varus stress indicates LCL insufficiency, the primary static restraint to varus load; because isolated LCL injury is uncommon, this finding should prompt screening for concurrent posterolateral corner or peroneal nerve involvement given the typical direct-varus mechanism.

Varus-loading alignment.text: Static or dynamic varus alignment reflects either the causative varus mechanism of injury or an inability of the compromised LCL/posterolateral structures to resist the varus moment during single-leg stance.

findings: Resisted tests around the knee usually painless
Passive varus stress (lateral gap) at 0°/30° positive — the definitive test
sttt.interpretation: Painless resisted testing is expected; passive varus stress (lateral gap) at 0°/30° is the definitive test for LCL sprain.

cpa.pattern: TFL/ITB and Biceps Femoris (lateral chain) often become protectively overactive — check TFL "Overactive, IT band syndrome" pattern once acute phase allows. Fascial component (from source): Lateral capsule / ITB fascia.

kineticChain.reason: Knee Valgus Stress Test is valgus-focused; this app's KC library has no dedicated varus-stress equivalent — rely on the passive varus-stress STTT test above.

functionalScreen.name: Forward Lunge (general sagittal-plane screen)
functionalScreen.note: A general sagittal-plane screen; no LCL-specific named functional test exists in this app's library. FMA source note: Varus stress & lateral loading reproduce pain.

Patellar maltracking.text: A laterally-deviated or laterally-tilting patella during active extension reflects an imbalance between medial (VMO) and lateral (vastus lateralis, ITB/lateral retinaculum) restraint forces, altering patellofemoral contact pressure and reproducing anterior knee pain.
Patellar maltracking.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.12; Witvrouw, patellofemoral pain literature

VMO wasting.text: Selective VMO atrophy relative to vastus lateralis has classically been theorized to allow unopposed lateral pull on the patella, though a systematic review and meta-analysis of VMO/VL firing-timing studies found inconsistent evidence for both the magnitude and direction of any true onset delay — the finding is clinically useful but its mechanistic explanation remains contested.
VMO wasting.source: Wong, "The relative timing of VMO and VL in the aetiology of anterior knee pain," systematic review and meta-analysis (PMC2386790)

No effusion.text: The absence of joint effusion helps differentiate PFPS — an extra-articular, retropatellar overload condition — from intra-articular pathology such as ACL or meniscal tear, or an OA flare, all of which typically present with swelling.

Dynamic valgus.text: Femoral adduction/internal rotation producing knee valgus during weight-bearing tasks dynamically increases the effective Q-angle and lateral patellofemoral shear force, a key driver of anterior knee pain distinct from the static Q-angle measured in supine.
Dynamic valgus.source: Powers, "The influence of altered lower-extremity kinematics on patellofemoral joint dysfunction"

Foot pronation.text: Excessive subtalar pronation drives compensatory tibial internal rotation that, transmitted proximally through the kinetic chain, increases dynamic knee valgus and lateral patellar tracking forces — a recognized distal contributor to PFPS.
Foot pronation.source: Tiberio, kinetic chain model of foot pronation and patellofemoral pain; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment

Femoral IR.text: Excessive femoral internal rotation, often from weak hip external rotators/gluteus medius, increases the dynamic Q-angle and lateral patellofemoral contact stress — the biomechanical rationale for proximal (hip) rather than purely local rehabilitation targeting in PFPS.
Femoral IR.source: Powers, "The influence of altered lower-extremity kinematics on patellofemoral joint dysfunction"

resisted.label: Resisted Knee Extension at 0–30° (VMO timing test)

findings: Resisted knee extension at 0–30° (VMO timing test) shows VL firing before/dominating VMO
Passive patellar glide shows a lateral bias / tight lateral retinaculum
sttt.interpretation: VL dominance over VMO on resisted testing plus a laterally-biased passive patellar glide is the classic PFPS maltracking pattern.

muscles.name: Glute Medius (hip)
muscles.state: Check — proximal weakness drives dynamic valgus

cpa.pattern: "Inhibited, VL dominant" is the textbook PFPS finding; also check Glute Medius (hip), since proximal weakness drives the dynamic valgus feeding PFPS. Fascial component (from source): Lateral retinaculum / ITB tightness.

kineticChain.name: Patellar Mobility Test
kineticChain.chainEffect: The direct match: "laterally biased, tight lateral retinaculum" is explicitly linked in the app's own data to "CPA: VMO inhibited → VL overactive."

functionalScreen.name: Wall-Slide PF-Compression Screen
functionalScreen.note: The named functional test for a PF pain arc. FMA source note: Single-leg decline squat & step-down reproduce anterior pain.

Inferior-pole tenderness.text: Point tenderness at the inferior pole of the patella localizes to the proximal patellar tendon origin — the classic 'jumper's knee' site — consistent with the reactive/degenerative tendon changes described in the Cook & Purdam continuum model at the point of greatest tensile and compressive load.
Inferior-pole tenderness.source: Cook & Purdam, "Is tendon pathology a continuum? A pathology model to explain the clinical presentation of load-induced tendinopathy" (2009)

Jumper's history.text: A history of repetitive jump-landing loading (volleyball, basketball) is the classic mechanism producing cumulative tensile overload at the patellar tendon origin, consistent with the load-induced pathogenesis central to the Cook & Purdam continuum model.

Stiff-landing posture.text: Landing with reduced knee flexion excursion decreases the eccentric shock-absorbing role of the quadriceps-patellar tendon complex, concentrating load over a shorter range and increasing peak tendon strain — a recognized biomechanical risk factor for patellar tendinopathy.
Stiff-landing posture.source: Cook & Purdam (2009); Cook et al., patellar tendinopathy load-management literature

Patellar tendon.text: Reproducing tenderness on direct palpation of the tendon (typically at the inferior pole) confirms the tendon as the primary pain generator, consistent with Cyriax's contractile-lesion localization and the structural correlate to symptoms described in the Cook & Purdam continuum model.
Patellar tendon.source: Cyriax, Textbook of Orthopaedic Medicine; Cook & Purdam (2009)

findings: Resisted knee extension strong but painful at the inferior-pole/patellar tendon — classic contractile-lesion pattern
sttt.interpretation: Strong-but-painful resisted knee extension localizing to the inferior pole is the classic Cyriax contractile-lesion pattern for patellar tendinopathy; a decline squat is the functional equivalent.

cpa.pattern: Overactive Rectus Femoris with VMO inhibition often accompanies jumper's knee; check VMO facilitation alongside tendon loading capacity. Fascial component (from source): Superficial front line (quad–patellar tendon).

kineticChain.name: Patellar Mobility Test (adjunct)

fields.label: Retinacular tension affecting tendon load line

kineticChain.chainEffect: Can be checked as an adjunct (retinacular tension affects tendon load line), but isn't primary here — the eccentric loading functional screen below is more direct.

functionalScreen.name: Eccentric Single-Leg Step-Down Screen
functionalScreen.note: The named functional test for reproducing tendon load pain. FMA source note: Decline single-leg squat loads and reproduces tendon pain.

Bony enlargement.text: Firm, bony enlargement along the joint line or peripatellar region reflects osteophyte formation, a hallmark palpable and radiographic feature of degenerative joint disease as articular cartilage loss triggers compensatory subchondral bone remodeling.

Effusion.text: Recurrent, often low-grade effusion in OA reflects synovial reaction to cartilage and bone debris and low-grade synovitis, distinguishing it from the acute traumatic hemarthrosis seen with an acute ligamentous injury.

Varus/valgus.text: Static frontal-plane malalignment (most commonly varus) reflects asymmetric compartmental cartilage loss — varus alignment both results from and accelerates medial compartment OA by concentrating load medially, a well-documented self-perpetuating cycle.
Varus/valgus.source: Sharma et al., malalignment and knee OA progression; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.12

Crepitus.text: Palpable or audible grinding during active or passive knee motion reflects loss of smooth articular cartilage and irregular subchondral bone/osteophyte contact, one of the most reliable clinical signs of degenerative joint disease.

Varus/valgus malalignment.text: Sustained frontal-plane malalignment during static stance and gait concentrates compressive load on the involved compartment (typically medial in varus OA), perpetuating cartilage degeneration — the postural correlate of the varus/valgus deformity noted on observation.
Varus/valgus malalignment.source: Sharma et al., malalignment and knee OA progression; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.12

findings: Resisted tests generally painless (non-contractile unless secondary tendinopathy)
Passive flexion/extension both restricted — capsular pattern (flexion >> extension)
sttt.interpretation: Painless resisted testing with a capsular-pattern restriction (flexion >> extension), leathery end-feel, and reduced patellar mobility with crepitus is the classic degenerative/osteoarthritic pattern.

muscles.name: Glute Medius (hip)
muscles.state: Often also inhibited, contributing to dynamic malalignment

cpa.pattern: VMO commonly inhibited with VL dominant, and Glute Medius (hip) often also inhibited contributing to dynamic malalignment — check both. Fascial component (from source): Global knee capsular fascia.

kineticChain.name: Patellar Mobility Test + Tibial Rotation Assessment
kineticChain.chainEffect: Crepitus with passive glide and restricted rotation both corroborate the capsular/degenerative picture.

functionalScreen.name: Double Leg Squat

fields.label: Pain onset angle and compensation strategy

functionalScreen.note: Bilateral loading to observe pain onset angle and compensation strategy (heel-rise, trunk lean). FMA source note: Capsular-pattern ROM loss; stairs & squat limited.

Lateral epicondyle tenderness ~30° flexi.text: Tenderness at the lateral femoral epicondyle at approximately 30° of flexion corresponds to the 'impingement zone' where the ITB (or, per the modern compression-model, its underlying innervated fat pad) crosses the epicondyle — the same anatomic zone probed by the Noble compression test.
Lateral epicondyle tenderness ~30° flexi.source: Noble compression test literature (Physiopedia; Orthofixar); modern ITB compression-model literature

Runner.text: Repetitive knee flexion-extension during running cyclically loads the ITB over the lateral epicondyle, and training-error factors (sudden mileage increase, downhill running, cambered surfaces) are classic aggravators, making a running history a key risk marker for this diagnosis.
Runner.source: PM&R KnowledgeNow, Iliotibial Band Syndrome overview

Hip-drop / adducted running posture.text: A contralateral pelvic drop with ipsilateral hip adduction during single-leg stance reflects gluteus medius weakness, increasing hip adduction and knee internal rotation and consequently ITB tension/compression over the lateral epicondyle with each stride — the documented mechanism behind the TFL-overactive, glute-medius-inhibited compensation pattern.
Hip-drop / adducted running posture.source: Fredericson et al., gluteus medius weakness and iliotibial band syndrome

passive.label: Ober's Test (passive hip-adduction restriction)
options: Positive — reproduces lateral knee pain with Noble compression

findings: Resisted tests around the knee usually painless
Ober's test positive — key provocation reproducing lateral knee pain with Noble compression
sttt.interpretation: Painless resisted testing is expected; Ober's test (passive hip-adduction restriction) is the key provocation, reproducing lateral knee pain when combined with Noble compression.

cpa.pattern: "Overactive, IT band syndrome" is the textbook driver, always compensating for an inhibited Glute Medius; this exact pairing is documented in the app's own data. Fascial component (from source): Lateral line (ITB/TFL) tension.

kineticChain.name: Tibial Rotation Assessment

fields.label: Tibial IR restriction / lateral chain tightness
options: Restricted tibial IR — lateral chain tightness

kineticChain.chainEffect: Explicitly documented: "restricted tibial IR, lateral chain tightness... biceps femoris and IT band restricting IR."

functionalScreen.name: Eccentric Single-Leg Step-Down Screen

fields.label: Repetitive knee flexion-extension under eccentric load

functionalScreen.note: ITBFS is classically provoked by repetitive knee flexion-extension under eccentric load, which this test reproduces directly. FMA source note: Noble/Ober positive; single-leg squat shows valgus.
